fields.mechanism: Inertia — the tendency of a system to persist in its current state, leading to inefficient energy usage when not actively counteracted.
fields.intervention: Add high-thermal-mass phase-change material (PCM) panels to the refrigerator's interior walls to introduce thermal inertia, so the cabinet holds its cold temperature longer during compressor-off cycles, reducing compressor cycling frequency while maintaining cooling capacity.
fields.expected_effect: Reduced average compressor runtime and lower total electricity consumption without sacrificing temperature stability or cooling performance.
fields.falsification_test: Run two identical refrigerators (one with PCM panels, one without) under the same load and ambient conditions; measure kWh over 24 hours and verify the PCM unit uses less energy while keeping internal temperature within the same ±1°C band.

fields.mechanism: Persistence of a consumption state that strengthens over time due to inertia.
fields.intervention: Replace active compressor cycling with a passive thermal-mass core (e.g., phase-change material) inside the refrigerator that maintains the cold state via thermal inertia, so the compressor only runs briefly to recharge the core rather than continuously.
fields.expected_effect: Reduced compressor run-time and energy draw while sustaining required cooling capacity, as the cold state persists passively between recharges.
fields.falsification_test: Compare energy consumption of a prototype with the passive thermal-mass core versus a standard refrigerator under identical door-opening and load profiles; if the prototype does not show ≥20% energy reduction while holding internal temperature within ±1°C of setpoint, the mechanism fails.

fields.mechanism: Inertia – the tendency of a system to resist change, leading to persistence of a state (here, inefficient energy usage).
fields.intervention: Add a high-thermal-mass phase-change material (e.g., a sealed water/gel pack) inside the refrigerator cavity to increase thermal inertia, damping temperature fluctuations and reducing compressor cycling frequency.
fields.expected_effect: Lower average compressor runtime and reduced total energy consumption while maintaining the required cooling capacity (temperature stays within safe bounds).
fields.falsification_test: Run two identical refrigerators under the same door-opening schedule and ambient temperature; add the thermal mass to one. Measure kWh over one week. If the modified unit does not consume less energy, the mechanism is not effective.

fields.mechanism: Thermal inertia (persistence of temperature) combined with acoustic streaming to disrupt stagnant boundary layers.
fields.intervention: Install an ultrasonic transducer inside the refrigerator cavity that emits low-frequency acoustic waves to induce acoustic streaming, breaking up thermal boundary layers and enhancing convective heat transfer, thereby reducing compressor duty cycle.
fields.expected_effect: Reduced energy consumption (higher efficiency) while maintaining required cooling capacity due to improved heat transfer and reduced thermal inertia effects.
fields.falsification_test: Measure refrigerator energy consumption over a 24-hour cycle with and without acoustic excitation under identical load and ambient conditions; if energy consumption does not decrease by at least 10%, the mechanism is falsified.

fields.mechanism: Persistence of electricity consumption habits that strengthens over time, causing inertia and inefficient energy usage.
fields.intervention: Implement an adaptive control loop in the refrigerator's compressor that detects persistent, habitual duty-cycle patterns (e.g., constant full-power operation regardless of thermal load) and deliberately breaks that inertia by modulating compressor speed and defrost timing based on real-time temperature differentials and door-open frequency, while preserving cooling capacity via a minimum duty-cycle floor.
fields.expected_effect: Reduced average energy consumption per cooling cycle (lower kWh/day) without violating the required temperature setpoint range, because the system no longer persists in a fixed inefficient operating habit but adapts to actual demand.
fields.falsification_test: Run two identical refrigerator units side-by-side under identical ambient and load profiles for 30 days; one with standard fixed-duty-cycle control, one with the habit-breaking adaptive loop. Measure daily kWh and internal temperature stability. The mechanism fails if the adaptive unit does not achieve at least 10% lower energy use while maintaining temperature within ±1°C of setpoint across all cycles.
